articles.title_orig: Uyghurs facing deportation by Thailand say they will be ‘like slaves’ in China
articles.title_zh: Uyghurs facing deportation by Thailand say they will be ‘like slaves’ in China
articles.content_orig:
Activists fear Bangkok will give in to pressure from Beijing despite reports of torture and human rights abuses against the mostly muslim ethnic minority
The deportation of two more Uyghurs to China from Thailand would put their lives in grave danger, activists have said, with one of the men saying he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back.
Last year, Thai authorities forcibly deported 40 Uyghur men to China despite pleas from the men themselves and the UN. The US and Canada had reportedly offered to resettle them , but Bangkok appeared to want to avoid upsetting Beijing. The UN has said the returnees’ whereabouts remain unknown.
Now, two more men fear becoming the latest victims of Beijing’s repressive crackdown against the largely Muslim ethnic group, condemned by the UN as a potential crime against humanity .
The girlfriend of one of the men said her boyfriend, whose name is being withheld for security reasons, told the Guardian he wanted to go “anywhere else but China”.
Human rights groups said two Uyghur men were at risk of deportation after recently being transferred to an immigration detention centre and they feared Thai authorities may once again give in to pressure from Beijing.
Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, called for the men to be allowed to travel to a safe third country. “Previous Thai governments have kept Uyghurs in inhumane detention for years and then complied with Beijing’s demands to send them to China, where they were forcibly disappeared,” she said.
The men had been serving a seven-year prison sentence for offences related to an attempted escape from immigration detention in January 2020. They were part of a group of more than 200 Uyghur men, women and children who were apprehended by Thai police in 2014 near the border with Malaysia after they fled from China.
Since 2014, women and children in the group have been released to Turkey, while the men have been deported to China, in separate batches, attracting criticism from the United Nations and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio.
Uyghurs, a Turkic minority mainly from the Xinjiang region in China, have been subjected to decades of oppressive and discriminatory treatment from the Chinese authorities. This has included the incarceration of hundreds of thousands of people in detention camps aimed at stamping out their cultural identity.
Beijing has defended its policies in Xinjiang as being aimed at poverty alleviation and counter-terrorism.
In July, Marzeyya Kasem’s (who asked to be referred to by her Islamic alias) boyfriend wrote to her in a letter that he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back to China. “Sometimes I thought why I’m a human being. What I do wrong against China … no want to go back to China,” he wrote. She shared the letter with a Thai rights group.
The two men facing imminent deportation reportedly pleaded their case to Thailand’s office of the National Human Rights Commission on Wednesday.
Relatives of Uyghurs have said the Chinese government was “paranoid about Uyghurs going to a safe country in large numbers and living together”, and preferred to have them deported.
It is not clear whether China has issued a formal extradition request for the two men. But Chaipruak Doungprapat, Thailand’s national security council chief, told reporters that the men, along with three other Uyghurs who are still in prison, had arrest warrants outstanding in China.
Some have questioned whether criminal warrants could be credible considering that at least one of them, Kasem’s boyfriend, was a minor when he left China. “If they are really wanted for a crime in China, why didn’t China immediately issue a [Interpol] red notice [when they were detained in 2014]?” asked Kasem.
Kasem believes that because Thailand was criticised for last year’s mass deportation, this time the authorities were trying to establish a more credible legal basis for the move.
A spokesperson for China’s foreign affairs ministry said: “The cooperation between China and Thailand in combating cross-border illegal and criminal activities such as smuggling is consistent with the laws of the two countries, international law and international practice.”
A spokesperson for Thailand’s foreign affairs ministry declined to comment.
Additional research by Rebecca Ratcliffe

articles.title_orig: Ex-military chief Gadi Eisenkot, opponent of Netanyahu, tapped to form government
articles.title_zh: Ex-military chief Gadi Eisenkot, opponent of Netanyahu, tapped to form government
articles.content_orig:
Knesset has been deadlocked since the election last month when Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority
Israel’s president has ⁠chosen Gadi Eisenkot, prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ⁠strongest rival, to ⁠try to ​form a new government, after a deadlocked election that left neither man ⁠with a clear path to power.
Isaac Herzog’s office said he had informed Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, on Saturday night “of his intention to task him with forming a government”.
It added that the formal appointment would take place in an official ceremony on Sunday at the president’s residence in Jerusalem.
“Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy,” Eisenkot wrote on X in his first reaction to the announcement of his designation.
Netanyahu ‌is fighting to hold on to office ‌after his religious-nationalist coalition lost its majority in an election on 27 October but still emerged as the largest bloc ‌in parliament.
Should Eisenkot succeed in forming a coalition, he would take over as prime minister from Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving premier.
Eisenkot’s wide-ranging opposition bloc won 48 of the Israeli parliament’s 120 seats in October elections, while Netanyahu’s camp secured 53, leaving neither with a majority.
During party consultations with Herzog, 66-year-old Eisenkot received the endorsements of both Arab-majority lists, who could now play kingmakers after making unprecedented gains in the vote.
But it remains unclear if Eisenkot’s bloc would accept support from the Arab lists in forming a government.
Eisenkot, the military chief of staff from 2015 to 2019, has set out to unite Israelis after Netanyahu’s divisive tenure, under which the country moved sharply to the right.
He has vowed to crack down on extremist West Bank settlers who have attacked Palestinians with impunity, decrying recent incidents as “Jewish terror” abetted by Netanyahu’s government.
But the military man is no peacenik. He opposes the creation of a Palestinian state and vowed to end Hamas’s rule in Gaza and destroy the Islamist movement’s military wing.
Commanding the military during the 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot devised the so-called “Dahiya doctrine”. The idea, named after a Beirut suburb heavily damaged in that war, involves Israel vowing to use massive force against civilian infrastructure in areas controlled by the Lebanese militant movement Hezbollah.
After his appointment, Eisenkot will have 28 days to come up with the 61 votes needed for a government. If he comes up short, Herzog can provide a 14-day extension before he has to offer the mandate to someone else.
If neither side succeeds, Israel will head to fresh elections. The country held five elections between 2019 and 2022 due to repeated deadlocks.

articles.title_orig: China US$300 dating app ‘marriage-or-refund’ guarantee sparks intense online buzz
articles.title_zh: China US$300 dating app ‘marriage-or-refund’ guarantee sparks intense online buzz
articles.content_orig:
One observer notes AI matchmaking could create happier marriages, helping lift society’s cynicism towards romance
In China’s competitive dating market, a new matchmaking start-up is staking its revenue on a bold wager: find true love, or get every penny back.
Launched in July, Liangpei AI charges an annual membership fee of 2,000 yuan (US$300), which is fully refundable if a user remains unmarried after three years.
The offer is an audacious challenge to a conventional business model built on keeping singles hooked. China’s online dating market reached 22.6 billion yuan (US$3.4 billion) in 2024, serving roughly 280 million users.

articles.title_orig: President Herzog taps Eisenkot to form coalition, but path remains fraught
articles.title_zh: President Herzog taps Eisenkot to form coalition, but path remains fraught
articles.content_orig:
Israel's president says he will task opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new coalition government.
Isaac Herzog has been holding talks with political parties after neither Eisenkot's bloc nor that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured a majority in Israel's parliament, known as the Knesset, following last week's election.
Eisenkot will now have 28 days to try to form a new administration, with a potential 14-day extension.
"Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy," the former military chief wrote on X.
No political party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, meaning all governments have been coalitions.
Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, while Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.
Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That positions them as potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.
Herzog said that, after consulting all parties during the week, he would give Eisenkot the first chance to form a government.
A statement from the president's office said he had informed both Eisenkot and Netanyahu of the decision.
Following consultations with delegations from the incoming Knesset members, Eisenkot received 67 recommendations for the premiership and Netanyahu 46, the statement said.
The president has broad discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition and does not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats.
The election results had implied three possible options for the formation of a government : a national unity administration involving both Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.
Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but there has been speculation that an agreement could be reached.
He could also attempt to reach a deal with ultra-Orthodox parties, but that too would be difficult.
There is precedent for a unity government. In 2020, following three deadlocked elections, Netanyahu and his centrist rival Benny Gantz agreed a power-sharing deal in which the leadership rotated between the two.
During his consultations with the parties, Herzog had said that to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable government, he expected "factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled".
In the period 2019 to 2022, one of the most politically fractured in Israeli politics, there were five separate elections as Netanyahu and his rivals struggled time and again to co-operate.

articles.title_orig: Grief in China as rare snow leopard cub Ling Xiaohan loses 26-day fight for life
articles.title_zh: Grief in China as rare snow leopard cub Ling Xiaohan loses 26-day fight for life
articles.content_orig:
The young animal’s death despite intensive medical care following its rescue has sparked an outpouring of mourning on social media platforms
Despite intensive treatment efforts, the five-month-old cub died from complications arising from a severe brain injury, the cause of which is unknown, according to a statement by the Qinghai Wildlife Rescue and Breeding Centre.
“The centre deeply regrets that it was unable to save Ling Xiaohan and will conduct a comprehensive review of the rescue efforts,” it said on Monday on the official social media account of Xining Wildlife Park, its subordinate unit.

articles.title_orig: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
articles.title_zh: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
articles.content_orig:
Perched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.
Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.
Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.
But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.
Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU).
But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.
Before it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.
Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.
Once there, they could eat sausages in the beer garden on the Obersalzberg at 1,834m (6,017ft) above sea level, overlooking the Alps.
Unlike Hitler's nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War Two and demolished in 1952, the Eagle's Nest survived the war.
Tens of thousands of tourists visited each season, providing an important source of income to the region.
In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by.
Around 15 years ago, a photo exhibit was opened in the Kehlsteinhaus about its history.
Although the Eagle's Nest itself was "largely destroyed" by the fire, according to police, the documentation centre survived unscathed.
The authorities have not commented on a possible motive, but a 33-year-old man with a history of mental illness has been detained in a secure psychiatric hospital on suspicion of arson.
Some feel this is the moment to allow the site to fade into history.
"It's been torched now. It's been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state," said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge.
That has happened with "quite a few other Nazi sites", he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler committed suicide: "The bunker was filled in with concrete and a children's playground put on the top of it on the ground."
The Kehlsteinhaus was just "a Nazi vanity project" since romanticised by the name Eagle's Nest, he said.
But Bavaria's authorities take a different view about the site's future.
Both the state's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus.
"We can hardly leave a ruin standing there," Herrmann said.
Sven Keller, head of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, believes it is important not to leave the site in ruins, as that could encourage Neo-Nazi pilgrims, who would be able to hike up there completely undisturbed.
"We have quite some experience at Obersalzberg with what happens if we clear those sites. Hitler's Berghof was demolished in the 1950s, and in our experience, this does not remove such sites from the mental maps of people," he told the BBC's Today programme.
Nor does he believe "a one-on-one reconstruction" of the site is possible, and Blume has made clear on Bavarian radio that "it should not and must not cost the taxpayer anything".
Herrmann said they would look for a sensible solution in consultation with historians, given the historically complex circumstances surrounding the building.
Heinemann, who also heads the Leibniz Institute for Contemporary History, believes full-scale reconstruction should be "out of the question".
"I rather think we can document the state left by the fire and also document the historical remains of the Kehlsteinhaus, and then reconstruct parts in a modern design, to make clear the different layers of time that can be seen in this building," she told the BBC.
Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era.
With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency.
A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban "stumbling stones" memorials - embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis.
In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used.
The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi pilgrims.
But others had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past.
As one resident of Braunau am Inn told me, it was a delicate balance between how much to remember and how much to forget.

articles.title_orig: Ocarina of Time review: Does Nintendo's Zelda remake match its original?
articles.title_zh: Ocarina of Time review: Does Nintendo's Zelda remake match its original?
articles.content_orig:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was finally released on Thursday, after years of rumours that Nintendo would remake the game - considered one of the best ever made.
IGN called it "the biggest game of the decade" in their review when it launched in 1998 on the N64, and it set the standard for 3D games.
A lot of the things we take for granted in modern games - such as riding a horse, fighting with a sword and shield, or locking on to enemies with the tap of a button - were pioneered or perfected in Ocarina of Time.
It received an almost perfect score from critics and, decades on, remains the highest-rated game in history on Metacritic, which aggregates reviews.
So how do you remake what many consider a masterpiece?
Those like me who grew up playing the original will feel right at home here.
Nintendo has decided against reinventing the wheel, instead producing something which plays very similarly to the N64 classic.
As I've said before , video game remakes are a bit different to film or TV - gaming fans often clamour for a new take on their favourites, hoping developers harness evolution in tech to make them fresh.
And games have come a long way in the almost 30 years since the original Ocarina of Time came out.
"When you compare the games in the past and the games in modern times, so to speak, the norms of what people expect from a game have evolved naturally," Nintendo producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi told me.
"In the past, games where the users may have needed more imagination to fill the blanks or the gaps are now clearly expressed through the graphics that they see on the screen."
But fancy graphics have come at a price - a pivot away from realism into something a bit more cartoonish. Some might even be disappointed by this, given the N64 game had quite horrifying elements in places.
One was the Skulltula House, a room where people had been morphed into human-spider hybrids.
"Back when we created the original Ocarina of Time, the means to convey or express ideas was limited compared with what we have now," series producer Eiji Aonuma - who worked on the original game - said.
"With regard to even the so-called scary elements, we strove to add a touch of the comical."
But he told the BBC that enhanced graphics and lighting capabilities unintentionally exaggerated the already-spooky Skulltula House and its potential to strike fear into players.
"When we carried out the test play, the testers were telling us, 'Oh, this is too scary'," he said. "So of course, in the end product, we've made the necessary adjustments so that we can retain the same balance that we had achieved in the original."
I spoke to a few YouTubers about the upcoming game to get their thoughts - and the response was overwhelmingly positive.
Mike Channell, co-editor of the YouTube channel Outside Xbox, said he believed the remake had been made "very meticulously" in the hopes of living up to fan expectations.
"Having played the game, it's clear that serious thought has gone into every decision, to the point where I'm not convinced this remake has taken any less time and effort than an all-new Zelda game," he said.
"Ocarina of Time is obviously one of the great video game experiences in the history of the medium, but I have no doubt this new version will be the best way to experience this story.
"It's fleshed out as a world, sumptuously detailed, and the controls match 21st-Century expectations."
Ed King, known as Zeltik to his 893,000 followers on YouTube, said "the level of detail and charm" in the Ocarina of Time remake stood out.
"The Forest Temple has always been my favourite Zelda dungeon: a mysterious, haunted mansion in the deep woods, a lost work of man slowly being reclaimed by nature," he said. "The remake really leans into the surreal, uncanny nature of the original dungeon."
And fellow YouTuber StrawHatMidas said it was the "perfect" way to "bring this classic back".
"Not only does the game pay homage to the Nintendo 64 original, but it also expands on the things that made it so memorable," he said. "Everything from the world and atmosphere to the controls and soundtrack feels like a love letter to the classic Zelda formula."
Nintendo has made some big changes, not least to the Water Temple - a dungeon about two thirds into the game.
Aonuma said, having worked on the original, this was what he personally wanted to change most due to its reputation for being "very, very difficult".
He said there was now "a greater facility in tackling" the dungeon, as players can now easily change a critical in-game item known as heavy boots and have "the ability to leverage the camera orientation".
I grew up playing Zelda on the N64, which pioneered the joystick - but nowadays two sticks is the standard, with one to move and one to control the camera.
As far as I'm concerned, being able to freely move the camera this time round was a significant improvement.
At times, the trip down memory lane was captivating. I knew where to go and what to do, thanks to a kind of muscle memory. However, on occasion that took away from the experience - with some tasks achieved too easily and some puzzles too quickly because I recalled their solutions.
Some people will love how similar it is, but I have to wonder if Nintendo has played things a bit too safe.
I don't think the developers see it that way.
"Even if the game may look different, we've maintained the essence that the original developers wanted to and hopefully conveyed through the original Ocarina of Time," Fujibayashi said.
Don't get me wrong - the game has lots of changes and surprises, and I won't spoil them, but I wish there had been more.
Then again, perhaps the best games leave you wanting more.
Or as Mike put it: "I loved the original as much as the next person, but I don't think I'll be going back to it."
Fans will no doubt wonder whether this is it, or if there will be more Zelda on the horizon. With the franchise's first movie coming next year, there's certainly more to come in the short term.
And in the long term, I wondered if with 30 more years of technological advancements, Nintendo might consider remaking the game once again.
"I will be long retired," Aonuma said, with a laugh.

articles.title_orig: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 in Ukraine as country prepares for talks with Russia and US
articles.title_zh: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 in Ukraine as country prepares for talks with Russia and US
articles.content_orig:
Moscow used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in attacks on electricity substations and bridge over the Dnipro
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.
Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.
Negotiators from Russia , Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.
Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said .
Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.
The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.
The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.
They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN , Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.
In a series of social media posts , Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.
after newsletter promotion
Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.
Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”
Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.
Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.

articles.title_orig: Judge orders Paraguay's ex-president Peña held before trial
articles.title_zh: Judge orders Paraguay's ex-president Peña held before trial
articles.content_orig:
Lee el artículo en español
Paraguay’s senate has voted to impeach President Santiago Peña, who is facing a criminal investigation and is under house arrest following the collapse of a major bank he had business links to.
The country’s Senate voted to remove him from office on Friday with 44 of the 45 members voting in favor. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as president soon after the impeachment vote.
Peña announced his resignation from office on Thursday after Ueno Bank was shut down overnight due to a solvency crisis, leaving millions of customers unable to access their money and triggering a scandal.
Paraguay’s Attorney General has opened three criminal cases against Peña and other former officials related to the bank crisis. The impeachment vote strips Peña of his parliamentary immunity.
Peña will remain under house arrest until a judge decides where he should stay while the criminal process against him takes place, according to prosecutor Christian Benítez.
The prosecutor’s office said it ordered Peña’s arrest in relation to the Ueno Bank crisis. CNN has reached out to Peña’s lawyers for comment.
The country’s lower chamber of Congress had accused him of “serious and systematic dereliction of duty” in connection with his dealings with the bank.
Although Peña himself was not present at the impeachment vote, his legal team represented him before Congress. Attorneys Adolfo Ferreiro and Ricardo Preda appeared in the Senate after lawmakers rejected a request from Peña for a 72-hour extension to prepare his defense.
Peña submitted his resignation while lawmakers were debating charges brought against him by 35 opposition lawmakers and ruling-party dissidents. The charges proposed “removing from office” the president, who took power in August 2023 for a five-year term.
Soon after he announced he would resign, Paraguay’s Chamber of Deputies voted unanimously to trigger impeachment proceedings.
“This guy, Santiago Peña, needs to be jailed. An arrest warrant must be issued … pretrial detention, straight to jail,” Senator Yolanda Paredes told reporters earlier.
Peña’s party, the right-wing Colorado Party, has a majority in both houses of Congress.
Peña said earlier that he was resigning to give peace of mind to Paraguayans “who entrusted their savings to our financial system.”
“I have made the decision to submit my resignation from the Presidency of the Republic. I do so with the stability of our country, social peace, and the need to preserve our public institutions in mind,” he said in a message posted on social media.
Peña entered office as one of the youngest presidents in Paraguayan history at the age of 44. He served as Minister of Finance from 2015 to 2017 during the presidency of Horacio Cartes and also served as a director of the Central Bank.
He is one of the staunchest allies of US President Donald Trump’s administration and has aligned with Trump’s political priorities, particularly on immigration and security.
In response to the president’s announced resignation, a US State Department spokesperson said the relationship between both countries remains strong: “We remain committed to the enduring relationship between the American and Paraguayan people and look forward to continuing our close cooperation on shared priorities.”
Paraguay’s president became embroiled in the crisis that erupted after the intervention of Ueno Bank, a private institution to which he has been linked and which, during his administration, received millions in funds from public entities, including the Social Security Institute (IPS), which manages the pensions of most of the country’s workers.
CNN contacted the presidency before Peña’s resignation to ask about the allegations against him.
The Central Bank of Paraguay found that Ueno Bank’s solvency ratio — with 2.9 million customers in a country of 6.1 million people — had fallen below 50% of the required minimum, “as a result of adjustments made to its financial statements during the regularization process.”
As a result of the resolution or dissolution proceedings, the savings of millions of customers were frozen at the financial institution, which is also known for sponsoring local soccer teams and Paraguay’s national team.
Attorney General Emiliano Rolón Fernández ordered the opening of three cases to investigate “the supervision and resolution of Ueno Bank SA, the placement of public funds in said entity and the actions of authorities from different State institutions.”
Paraguay was shaken by Tuesday’s intervention of Ueno, an institution that, according to authorities, violated limits on loans to related companies.
Paraguay’s Central Bank said Thursday night it would start processing guarantee payments to certain Ueno customers in stages.
Peña announced his resignation after two days of long lines at banks, anxiety and street protests.
The country has been trying to position itself as a regional financial hub by capitalizing on the investment-grade status it attained in recent years, after receiving approval from two of the world’s leading rating agencies.
This is a developing story and will be updated.
CNN’s Mauricio Torres, Ivonne Valdés Garay and Jennifer Hansler contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: 7 4-Cylinder Cars With More Horsepower Than A Ford Mustang EcoBoost
articles.title_zh: 7 4-Cylinder Cars With More Horsepower Than A Ford Mustang EcoBoost
articles.content_orig:
When Ford gave its iconic Mustang a dramatic redesign for the 2015 model year, the car came with a lot of big changes. One came out back, where the Mustang moved to a standard independent rear suspension for the first time in its existence. Another big change came under the hood, where Ford added the turbocharged 2.3-liter EcoBoost engine as the Mustang's volume engine option. A couple years later, with the old V6 dropped from the lineup, the EcoBoost four-cylinder became — and still is — the Mustang's base engine.
However, despite being the base engine, and despite upsetting some Mustang purists with its lack of displacement, it's hard to argue the Mustang's 2.3 EcoBoost is lacking in the horsepower department. The base model 2026 Mustang EcoBoost is rated at 315 horsepower, which is in fact, the same horsepower rating as the 2010 V8-powered Mustang GT, with the EcoBoost also outpowering previous V8 Mustang GTs of the '90s and 2000s as well.
The latest Ford Mustang EcoBoost is a car that shows just how far four-cylinder performance has come, but on the modern enthusiast market, it's not even the most powerful four-cylinder option.. To demonstrate this, we've rounded up five different four-cylinder vehicles that outgun the Mustang in horsepower rating, with a mix of cars that includes everything from hot hatchbacks to sport sedans, and even a crossover SUV.
Back in the '90s and '2000s, high-performance Honda and Acura vehicles were known for their unique, high-revving naturally aspirated engines. Today, though, Honda has fully embraced turbocharging, and the powerful Honda Civic Type R is known as one of the fastest front-wheel-drive cars in the world. In terms of horsepower ratings, the 2.0-liter turbocharged four-cylinder powering the latest Civic Type R ties the Mustang EcoBoost with the same 315-horsepower rating, but Honda builds another hot hatchback that actually edges both of them out in the power department.
That car is the highly enjoyable Acura Integra Type S, which is a closely related and slightly more upmarket sibling to the Civic Type R, using the same platform and the same 2.0-liter turbo engine. While the Acura and Honda engines are basically identical, the Integra uses a more aggressive exhaust system, which boosts its output by five horsepower, for a total of 320.
Head-to-head comparisons between the two Honda products show that the Integra's isn't enough to give the heavier Acura an edge in performance, but both cars are still considered among the best hot hatchbacks you can buy. Notably, the Integra Type S is very well matched against the Mustang EcoBoost in performance metrics, leaving buyers to choose between the Acura's precision and practicality or the Ford's rear-drive personality.
With American automakers being world-famous for their V8 engines, you'd expect most of the Mustang EcoBoost's top four-cylinder rivals to come from German or Japanese brands, and that's the case for most of the picks in this selection. However, Ford's arch-rival, General Motors, also has a very potent, four-cylinder engine of its own — and both larger and more powerful than the Ford 2.3. That engine is GM's 2.7-liter turbocharged four-cylinder, which is known as the L3B.
The 2.7 turbo is primarily found in Chevrolet and GMC pickup trucks, where its 310-horsepower rating comes in just below the Mustang EcoBoost's output. However, in the high-performance Cadillac CT4-V sport sedan , the L3B gets a few tweaks that push its peak output to 325 horsepower. The four-cylinder-powered CT4-V isn't on the the same level as the flagship CT4-V Blackwing with its twin-turbo V6, but the regular CT4-V is still very quick, capable of hitting 60 miles per hour in less than five seconds.
With the Cadillac CT4 being discontinued at the end of the 2026 model year, GM will have to hand the four-cylinder horsepower crown back to Ford, at least for the time being. Speculation suggests that GM is hard at work on a new lineup of rear-drive models, potentially including a reborn version of the Mustang's longtime rival, the Chevrolet Camaro. If and when those new GM models arrive, we wouldn't be surprised to see a turbo four-cylinder engine option that's at least equal to the current L3B.
Viewed as a whole, today's market doesn't have nearly the same number of affordably priced performance cars that we saw in decades past — but at least the hot hatchback segment is alive and well, with several great choices for enthusiasts. One of these choices is the Volkswagen Golf R, which pushes Volkswagen's four-cylinder performance to a new level.
Sharing its DNA with the iconic Golf GTI, the Golf R elevates the GTI's performance in a big way, adding an all-wheel-drive system and giving Volkswagen's turbocharged 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine a major bump in power. Already quick to start, Volkswagen updated the Golf R for the 2025 model year, which boosted its output to a stout 328 horsepower. With that aforementioned 4Motion AWD system, this well-appointed Volkswagen can rocket to 60 miles per hour in the low four-second range, making the Golf R one of the quickest and most mature hatchbacks you can buy .
Additionally, if we are going to talk about the Golf R, we also have to mention its closely related corporate cousin, the Audi S3. The S3 essentially puts the Golf R's powertrain into a sedan, and has the same 328-horsepower rating as its Volkswagen counterpart. With these German offerings, buyers can choose their preferred brand and body style, but in either case they'll be getting one of the most potent four-cylinder engines on the market today.
With the legendary reputation of the Porsche 911 and its flat-six engine, some car enthusiasts might not associate Porsche with high-powered four-cylinder engines, but Porsche has made a good few of those as well. The company has a long history of building impressive four-piston motors, and the engine from the Porsche 718 Cayman S and its Boxster S sibling is among the most powerful road-going examples around.
Displacing 2.5 liters, the flat-four engine that powers the 718 Cayman and Boxster S is rated at an even 350 horsepower. When the car debuted in 2017, during Car & Driver's testing, the Cayman S hit 60 miles per hour in just 3.6 seconds. What's also unique about the 718's four-cylinder engines is that, unlike the Mustang's EcoBoost 2.3 and the other inline-four engines on this list, the Porsche flat-four design is unique specifically to the Cayman and Boxsters, and not shared with other mainstream models.
Sure, some Porsche fans might recommend that you skip the four-cylinder models and go straight for the wonderful, flat-six-powered Cayman GTS or GT4, and there are lots of reasons one might want to do that. However, both when viewed on its own merits and when compared to other four-cylinder engines on the market, the Porsche 2.5 is easily among the best out there.
Given their relatively small displacement, it's no surprise that the engines on this list — including the Ford 2.3 EcoBoost itself — all use turbocharging to hit their impressive power levels. Toyota, though, has a potent 2.5-liter four-cylinder-powered vehicle that beats the Mustang's output without using a turbocharger.
Instead, the powertrain in the 2026 Toyota RAV4 Plug-In Hybrid uses a combination of an internal combustion four-cylinder engine and three electric motors to make a combined total of 324 horsepower. The result is one of the quickest mainstream compact crossover SUVs you can buy, capable of hitting 60 miles per hour in the low five-second range.
Sure, the RAV4 PHEV's high curb weight and family crossover DNA might keep it from ever being a serious performance machine in the way other cars on this list might be, but the unexpected nature of its horsepower is part of the fun. Beyond that, the RAV4 PHEV's powerful setup shows that hybrid electrification can be just as transformative as adding a turbocharger to a four-cylinder engine. In the case of the RAV4,

articles.title_zh: Google Messages homepage redesign: Pinned chat avatars, bottom search, corner Gemini
articles.content_orig:
In addition to the new app icon , Google Messages for Android is testing a big homepage redesign that has three core components.
Update 11/7 : Instead of pinned chats just appearing at the top of the list, Google Messages is trying a redesign that significantly elevates them above all conversations.
This redesign takes advantage of the existing background layer that’s currently just home to the logo/wordmark, search, and account menu.
You’ll see large contact photos appear above all chats, which pushes the list of other conversations down the page. Like iMessage on iOS, this layout has the downside of not showing any history or last sent information.
Meanwhile, Google is testing another change where search becomes a centered floating action button (FAB) alongside new chat. When you’re scrolling down the page, you’ll see “Search” in a pill-shaped button, with the other button minimized.
Hate the idea of just the pinned "bobble head" look. I like being able to view message tidbits.  Plus, it's directly copying Apple (enough said). I have to use an iPhone at my job. I hate the pinned bubble conversation look and more importantly it's function.
Otherwise, you’ll see a circular magnifying glass icon and “Start chat” in the pill. The animation that accompanies this change looks nice and feels alive, while boosting one-handed usability.
Google has replaced the Gemini FAB with a button in the top-right corner next to your profile image. This matches the design leveraged by Workspace apps on desktop and mobile.
These updates are currently in the beta channel and not yet widely rolled out to all testers. Some users have all aspects of the redesign, but it appears that Google is rolling out the various components in a piecemeal fashion.

articles.title_orig: King Charles would ‘carefully’ consider China visit
articles.title_zh: King Charles would ‘carefully’ consider China visit
articles.content_orig:
By REBECCA ENGLISH, ROYAL EDITOR and GLEN OWEN
Published: 18:29 EDT, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 18:59 EDT, 7 November 2026
King Charles would be prepared to undertake a controversial state visit to China if requested by Prime Minister Andy Burnham , sources indicated on Saturday.
As Charles is recovering from his 'challenging' Caribbean tour dominated by rows over slavery reparations, Buckingham Palace was not ruling out an even more politically testing trip to Beijing .
Such a visit would be the first by a British monarch to the communist country for 40 years, but would be fraught with controversy given the ongoing security threat posed by China to Britain. One Whitehall source told The Mail on Sunday: 'We understand the King would be quite up for it, if it came to it.'
But a senior Tory source said: 'This would be seen as seriously divisive politics.'
Royal insiders stress a trip isn't on the table yet and would come with 'complex' logistical and political issues to navigate.
As Prince of Wales, Charles made no secret of his antipathy to the Chinese regime. But a royal aide said: 'If the government said 'Will the King go to China?' I think we would think about it very carefully.
'China is a hugely important country... a very complex country. It would pose a lot of complexity in putting a programme together. This is the 40th anniversary of the last state visit.'
It comes amid a battle within the Government over whether to confront or appease Beijing. Security officials have complained that Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is leading the 'appease' camp as the UK is so reliant on China for the supply of solar panels central to his Net Zero climate agenda.
King Charles III during his tour of Antigua and Barbuda. The Palace has not ruled the King travelling on a politically testing trip to Beijing
Prime Minister Andy Burnham. A battle is raging within the Government over whether to confront or appease Beijing
As heir to the throne, Charles maintained a highly–critical stance over the Chinese government, particularly as a result of his support for Tibet and the Dalai Lama. He boycotted UK state banquets for presidents Jiang Zemin in 1999 and Hu Jintao in 2005 over China's human rights record.
He once described Chinese officials as 'appalling old waxworks', and also wriggled out of a state banquet to honour president Xi Jinping in 2015.
Despite mounting evidence of state–sponsored activities in the UK, such as cyber attacks and political infiltration, Mr Miliband supports closer ties with China. One of his first moves as Foreign Secretary was to arrange to meet Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi.
Former Tory leader Iain Duncan Smith said: 'If it is true the King might be going to China it is utterly appalling. They are effectively at war with us, and should not be rewarded for it.'
Diplomats believe the King's Caribbean tour was a success, particularly his visit to Guyana, where he was welcomed with open arms at a time when China is making huge inroads in the region.
If rumours are correct, the King is to be wheeled out as Britain's version of 'panda diplomacy' and sent to Communist China.
Is this a state visit too far? I think it is. The issue is not Charles. He has shown himself a master of sensitive visits, whether to the US under erratic Donald Trump or to the Caribbean, where slavery reparations dominated discussion.
No, the question is: why are we debasing ourselves by offering a visit to a China leadership that behaves so destructively towards us? It would be ironic. The debate about historic slavery in the Caribbean pales against China's record of using forced labour now in its cotton and potentially other industries, including silicon used in solar panels that Net Zero fanatic Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband wants to cover the British countryside with. And we reward this with a state visit?
Too often our leaders, especially on the Left, continue the delusion that China is an economic El Dorado which will make us rich. But Beijing does not want free trade. It wants to make others dependent on it. This is not trade as a tool of joint prosperity but trade as a weapon in conflict.
Rather than organising a cringeworthy visit, our leaders' time would be better spent standing up for our values and interests and articulating them clearly.

articles.title_orig: New Zealand’s election results are too close to call
articles.title_zh: New Zealand’s election results are too close to call
articles.content_orig:
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, on 5.
The electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Kipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests.
The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens – who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops – saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

articles.title_orig: California college system drops $193M on sprawling cliffside hotel — as in-state students fork over $50K a year on tuition
articles.title_zh: California college system drops $193M on sprawling cliffside hotel — as in-state students fork over $50K a year on tuition
articles.content_orig:
California students are getting slammed with college bills topping $50,000 a year — while the University of California system is dropping nearly $200 million on a luxury hotel overlooking the Pacific Ocean.
UC Investments, the university system’s investment arm, has purchased the Ritz-Carlton in Half Moon Bay for a whopping $193 million, according to a report by Coastside News .
The 261-room coastal resort will join UC Investments’ portfolio, which is valued at more than $300 billion and helps fund retirement benefits and pensions for roughly 40,000 university retirees.
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
UC representatives declined to comment to the outlet.
The eye-popping purchase comes as the cost of attending several UC campuses has surged past $50,000 annually for California residents, raising fresh questions about affordability at a public university system long viewed as a pathway to an affordable college education.
The hotel deal could also come with some financial baggage. Its previous owner reportedly owed as much as $2.1 million in overdue hotel occupancy taxes.
Unlike university-owned hotels typically used for conferences and academic retreats, the Half Moon Bay Ritz-Carlton is intended strictly as an investment, a source told Coastside News.
The university could keep the Ritz-Carlton name and bring in the luxury brand’s management team to operate the property, according to another source who owns multiple hotels.
The resort is also a major player in the local economy, serving as Half Moon Bay’s largest employer and taxpayer, according to the report.
UC chief investment officer Jagdeep Singh Bachher has previously expressed interest in investing in local real estate, particularly in the Bay Area and affordable workforce housing, Coastside News reported.
The sprawling oceanfront property opened in 2001 and features 261 rooms, a full-service spa, multiple restaurants and sweeping views of the Pacific.
When it first opened, the resort boasted 93 fireplaces, six tennis courts and a 122-seat restaurant, with rooms reportedly going for as much as $3,000 a night.
But the plush property has also faced controversy over its coastal location, including concerns about erosion and rising sea levels.
Locals fought the resort’s development for decades, and in 2019 it was hit with a $1.6 million fine for blocking public access to a nearby beach.
The purchase comes as the UC system faces mounting pressure over its operating costs, including growing pension and retirement benefit expenses.
Housing and food costs have also helped drive up the price of a college education, leaving California families facing six-figure bills for a four-year degree at a public university.
Over four years, many in-state families will spend about $200,000, while out-of-state students can pay more than $300,000 when factoring in other costs like housing.

articles.title_orig: "Congress will investigate": Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces probe over alleged Chinese spy ties
articles.title_zh: "Congress will investigate": Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces probe over alleged Chinese spy ties
articles.content_orig:
Three House Republican committee leaders asked Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to sit for a closed-door briefing on his relationship with a tech executive reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang unveiled Thursday, using the acronym for the People's Republic of China.
They are seeking information on Huang's interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage," they wrote in the brief message, which is dated Wednesday.
The letter does not specify which reports it is referring to. But The New York Times reported last week that U.S. intelligence found Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen determined to be funneling information to Beijing, had "developed a close relationship" with Jensen Huang.
President Donald Trump , who himself has forged close ties with Jensen Huang as he champions the U.S. artificial intelligence industry, was briefed about a year ago on those intelligence findings, the Times reported.
Trump "chose not to do anything with the information," according to the newspaper, which cited interviews with people briefed on the surveillance and other sources.
The letter to Huang was signed by House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark.
Nvidia did not directly respond when asked by CNBC to comment on the letter and confirm whether Huang would attend the lawmakers' proposed briefing.
Nvidia instead provided a statement that largely mirrored the one it previously sent the Times, in which a spokesperson suggested Jensen Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were no different from his meetings with other executive clients.
"Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security," the spokesperson said in the statement.
"Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," the spokesperson said. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know."
A spokeswoman for Mast did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for additional information. Megaspeed did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.
The lawmakers invited the Nvidia CEO to appear for an in-person joint briefing on Nov. 18. Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17.
"China's access to that sensitive U.S. tech is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the committee leaders wrote. "It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk."

articles.title_orig: Berkshire Hathaway speeds up stock buybacks, though profit falls
articles.title_zh: Berkshire Hathaway speeds up stock buybacks, though profit falls
articles.content_orig:
Berkshire Hathaway said Saturday it accelerated its share repurchases during the third quarter, as operating and overall profits took a hit.
The Greg Abel-led conglomerate bought back $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock. That's more than double the $4.5 billion repurchased in the second quarter and brings the company's total buybacks for 2026 to about $14.4 billion.
The sharp increase came as Berkshire's operating earnings — those from wholly-owned businesses — fell year over year, as profits from its insurance business pulled back.
Berkshire operating profits totaled $12.705 billion, down 5.8% from $13.485 billion in the year-earlier period. Insurance underwriting tumbled 43% year on year to $1.352 billion, while insurance investment income declined 14% to $2.734 billion. Berkshire's railroad, energy and manufacturing businesses all saw earnings grow year over year.
The company's overall earnings, which include Berkshire's sprawling stock market portfolio, also dropped 28% in the third quarter to $22.112 billion from $30.796 billion a year prior. Investment gains for the company fell nearly 50% to $9.407 billion.
Despite the earnings pullback, Berkshire stock has outperformed recently amid a massive rotation out of technology stocks. Class A shares are up more than 12% over the past month, while the S&P 500 has dropped 5.5% in that time. Year to date, Berkshire has gained 13%, while the broad market index is up just 7.8%.
Berkshire's five largest equity holdings remained the same in the third quarter: Alphabet , American Express , Apple , Bank of America and Coca-Cola .
Berkshire's cash hoard also grew 3% in the third quarter $377.435 billion from $365.514 billion in the second quarter. However, excluding rail and utility cash along with T-bill payables, the conglomerate's cash holdings totaled $352.3 billion, down 1.9% quarter over quarter.
— CNBC's Alex Crippen contributed reporting.

articles.title_zh: 'Backglow' Lets You Customize New MacBook Pro's Glowing Apple Logo
articles.content_orig:
A new "Backglow" app created by designer Juan Buis lets you customize the illuminated Apple logo on the lid of the new MacBook Pro models.
The free version of the app allows you to manually adjust the brightness level of the Apple logo, independent of the MacBook Pro's display brightness level. You can also turn it off entirely with a single click, rather than having to use Terminal .
Another free option is a "Breathe" mode that makes the logo's light gently pulse similarly to the sleep indicator light on older MacBooks.
A one-time payment unlocks the Pro version of the app: $9 for a limited time or $15 later. This gives you two additional modes: "Music" mode makes the logo's light move to the beat of the music you play on your Mac, while "Agents" mode makes the light pulse while Claude Code is working and blinks when your attention is needed.
here's what it can do:
- manually set logo brightness (apple doesn't let you) - breathe slowly, like the old mac sleep light - pulse to your music - blink when claude needs you - turn the logo light off with one click
try it here: https://t.co/WZTWMq5yAf https://t.co/FI0o9ayKBZ
— juan (@juanbuis) November 6, 2026
Daring Fireball 's John Gruber was told that Apple engineered a "custom light source just to enable the logo to glow once again, without adding any additional thickness to the lid." Why? "Because it's awesome," he heard an Apple representative say.
By default, Apple says the logo is illuminated whenever the Mac is awake. It automatically brightens or dims based on the screen's brightness level and your environment's lighting conditions detected by the computer's ambient light sensor.
Buis said the logo is lit by a white LED that does not change colors.

articles.title_orig: CoreWeave Asks Texas Governor-Elect for Data Center Cooperation
articles.title_zh: CoreWeave Asks Texas Governor-Elect for Data Center Cooperation
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said on Thursday that the state will introduce laws to protect its residents with regards to data centers, ‌citing their impact on rural communities.
With plentiful energy supplies, relatively cheap land and a ‌pro-business policy, Texas has become one of the leading regions in the world for data center developments.
"Data centers have ​moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans," Democrat Hinojosa, who beat Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in Tuesday's election, told CNN in an interview.
"We will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data ‌centers until we have those ⁠protections," she said, adding that communities should have "a seat at the table" on if and how data centers operate in their areas.
US President Donald ⁠Trump's administration has strongly backed data center expansion as a national priority, but the public is increasingly opposed to such projects, citing concerns about electricity demand, water consumption, wildlife impacts and public access ​to federal ​lands.
Abbott became one of the first Republican governors ​in the US to halt the ‌connection of new data centers to the state's electric grid and ordered a comprehensive audit of the projects.
Hinojosa has rattled the state's data center industry with a campaign pledge to halt new projects.
Billionaire Elon Musk supported Abbott in the election and had spent $158 million to promote Texas Republican US Senate candidate Ken Paxton alone, Musk said on Wednesday.
Musk's SpaceX and Tesla are headquartered ‌in the Lone Star State, where he is also ​planning a chipmaking venture.
Texas can also have a strong ​working relationship with Musk and his companies, ​but on her administration's terms, Hinojosa added.
In October, publication Texas Monthly reported ‌that the state had been discussing the ​sale of Boca Chica ​State Park to SpaceX, citing sources.
During a news conference on Thursday, Hinojosa said she had spoken to the executive director of the Texas Parks and Wildlife Commission "to request ​that no action be taken" ‌while there is an ongoing transition from Abbott to her.
SpaceX did not immediately ​respond to a request for comment from Reuters.
(Reporting by Costas Pitas and Bhargav ​Acharya; Editing by Daphne Psaledakis and Christopher Cushing)

articles.title_orig: South Africa's ANC facing worst-ever performance in local elections
articles.title_zh: South Africa's ANC facing worst-ever performance in local elections
articles.content_orig:
South Africa's African National Congress (ANC) is heading for an historically poor election performance , with the near-final tally from Wednesday's municipal polls showing it coming in with just over 30% of the vote.
The ANC also lost its majority in six of the eight metropolitan regions, South Africa's Electoral Commission said Saturday in sharing the results after 98% of votes were counted.
South African voters in 2026 are angry about water and electricity shortages, with the ANC taking the blame for the poor state of municipalities.  High unemployment, crime, and widespread corruption are other pressing issues.
ANC leader, and South African president, Cyril Ramaphosa , has not yet addressed the poor performance as of Saturday evening. However, during the week, he admitted in his weekly presidential letter that "municipal failures have contributed to declining public trust and confidence in democratic governance."
On Saturday, ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula told reporters that the ANC needs to work on winning back public confidence.
"We cannot ask the people to trust us merely because of our history," Mbalula said.
"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC ... as much as we are the largest party, it has been catastrophic for the movement," he added.
Although the ANC will still be the single largest party by overall vote percentage, it had governed with an absolute majority for most of its history up until the general election in 2024 saw it lose an outright parliamentary majority for the first time in South Africa's democratic era.
"This is the most severe result that the ANC would have feared," political analyst Daniel Silke told the AFP news agency.
"It's the ANC's worst result in history," Silke said, adding that the result will undermine the ANC's ability to exert authority on the local and national level. The results could also provide a bellwether of voter sentiment ahead of the 2029 general elections.
Once led by Nelson Mandela , the ANC was instrumental in ending apartheid, and took and power in 1994 after South Africa became a democracy.
But over the past decade, it has steadily performed worse in one election after another. In 2024, the ANC secured just over 40% in the 2024 national polls and 46% at the previous municipal elections in 2021.
After losing the absolute majority in 2024, the ANC formed a cross-party national unity government with all the parties represented in parliament, which is still in power.
The ANC's decline comes amid disillusionment over corruption, mismanagement and high unemployment. Smaller parties have also emerged across South Africa's political landscape, cutting into the ANC's voter base.
South Africa is now looking at complex coalition negotiations for municipal level governing alliances.
Runner up in the polls looks to be the pro-business, center-right Democratic Alliance (DA), coming in at 24% of the votes.
The DA is set to keep control of Cape Town after winning an absolute majority. It also performed well in the capital, Pretoria, and economic hub of Johannesburg, and is expected to form coalitions that exclude the ANC.
"All of the cut and thrust that comes with the election is now over, and it is time now... to put together governments that can actually fix these towns and cities," DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis told reporters.
"We have already reached out to many parties over the last 24 hours and will continue to do so today," he said.

articles.title_orig: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and under house arrest
articles.title_zh: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and under house arrest
articles.content_orig:
Prosecutors in Paraguay have charged former president Santiago Peña over his alleged role in a banking scandal that led to his impeachment.
He has been accused of breach of trust and administration for personal gain.
Peña, who denies any wrongdoing, was forced from office after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.
He was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.
He had offered to step down but rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.
Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.
The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.
Peña's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.
"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.
The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.
Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.
An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, Asunción.
Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.
Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.
Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.
"It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," Peña said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".
Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".
Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history – a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image."
Analysts say Peña is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse.
His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic".

articles.title_orig: Scientists Discover Two Enormous Tears in a Tectonic Plate Beneath Iran
articles.title_zh: Scientists Discover Two Enormous Tears in a Tectonic Plate Beneath Iran
articles.content_orig:
On the scale of human generations, the tectonic plates that form Earth's crust and upper mantle are moving incredibly slowly.
They are constantly moving, though, and across millions of years, that movement leads to some globally significant shifts in the landscape.
Researchers led by a team from the Chinese Academy of Sciences have now found extensive evidence of two giant tears in a tectonic plate called the Arabian Plate, underneath southeastern Iran.
The tears are being caused by different rock densities. One part of the plate is what's known as an oceanic slab and was once part of the ancient Neo-Tethys Ocean.
The basalt rock here is heavier and thinner and is being pushed under a neighboring plate (the process of subduction).
Meanwhile, the other part of the plate is continental rock – thicker in size but less dense in composition, with lighter ingredients that make it granite-like.
This rock doesn't like to be pushed underground, and instead forms mountains when it hits resistance. That mismatch is what's causing the ruptures.
In a new study published in Nature Geoscience , the researchers have detailed their findings, explaining how the discoveries give us a new perspective on how oceans disappear and continents collide as tectonic plates shift.
What's more, there's a good chance these tears will eventually meet.
"The coexistence of these two tearing modes provides a rare snapshot of the short-lived early transition from oceanic subduction to continental collision," write the researchers in their published paper.
To measure geological activity deep underground, the researchers used a network of 69 different seismic monitoring stations to detect the vibrations coming from distant earthquakes.
As these vibrations change speed based on rock temperature and density, a picture of tectonic plate activity can be put together.
The recordings, taken between March 2017 and September 2018, revealed the two tears: one horizontal (where the Zagros collision zone meets the Makran subduction zone), and a smaller vertical one, closer to the surface (by the Makran Trench).
"We show that in the Makran subduction zone, the oceanic lithosphere has continuously subducted to depths of at least 450 km, whereas in the Zagros collision zone to the west, the continental lithosphere has subducted no deeper than 300 km, resulting in east–southward slab tearing and detachment," write the researchers.
"We further identify another slab tear that probably initiated at the junction between the Makran Trench and the transform boundary and has propagated southward as the continental plate advances northward."
That second tear is more due to the movement of the plates than the differences between the oceanic and continental rock, the researchers suggest – but seeing them both at the same time in the same region is very unusual for geologists.
These rips in the plates have been progressing for several million years, according to the study models, and those same models indicate that it's likely that they'll eventually meet each other.
"While the two tears initiate independently, the intervening continental-oceanic boundary segment is progressively consumed as tearing advances," write the researchers.
"This progressive linkage is expected to eventually drive coalescence of the two tears."
The next question is how the tears, and their possible merging, might go on to affect volcanic activity in the region. It appears that hot magma is already filling some of the gaps caused by the ruptures.
We might have left planet Earth by the time the tears do combine, but for geologists today it's a rare look at these forces in action, particularly the final stages of the Neo-Tethys ocean – part of the Wilson Cycle that describes how oceans are made, expand, and then gradually vanish as tectonic plates move around.
"The transition from oceanic subduction to continental collision is a key stage in the Wilson Cycle," write the researchers.
"Yet, key processes governing this transition remain unclear owing to sparse observations of structure at depth."
The research has been published in Nature Geoscience .
This article was fact-checked by Peter Dockrill and edited by Peter Dockrill . While we pride ourselves on our process, we are only human. If you spot a mistake, please let us know .
