articles.title_orig: ‘Very strange, very sad’: Paraguay bank collapse fells a presidency and leaves millions broke
articles.title_zh: ‘Very strange, very sad’: Paraguay bank collapse fells a presidency and leaves millions broke
articles.content_orig:
Late night political drama as PeÃ±a is impeached and arrested
Prosecutors in Paraguay have charged former president Santiago PeÃ±a over his alleged role in a banking scandal that led to his impeachment.
He has been accused of breach of trust and administration for personal gain.
PeÃ±a, who denies any wrongdoing, was forced from office after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.
He was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.
He had offered to step down but rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached PeÃ±a and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.
PeÃ±a, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.
The impeachment charges that led to PeÃ±a's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.
PeÃ±a's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.
"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.
The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.
Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.
An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, AsunciÃ³n.
Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.
Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.
PeÃ±a's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.
"It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," PeÃ±a said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".
Afterwards, senate president Basilio NÃºÃ±ez said PeÃ±a was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".
Pedro Alliana takes the oath of office as interim President
Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history â a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image."
Analysts say PeÃ±a is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse.
His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic".

articles.title_orig: GE Aerospace Reports US$12.9bn in China Agreements
articles.title_zh: GE Aerospace Reports US$12.9bn in China Agreements
articles.content_orig:
A global review of commercial flight
SHANGHAI — GE Aerospace said November 6 that it had signed sales and service agreements worth more than US$12.9bn at the China International Import Expo, including engines and long-term support for China Eastern Airlines (MU).
Reuters reported the aggregate value and scope of the agreements , citing a GE Aerospace statement. The total covers multiple sales and service arrangements, rather than the price of China Eastern's new-aircraft engines alone.
China Eastern will purchase 202 LEAP-1A engines for 101 Airbus A320neo-family aircraft, Reuters reported. A separate agreement covers 14 spare engines across the LEAP-1A, LEAP-1C and CFM56-7B models. GE Aerospace also reached supply and repair agreements with MTU Maintenance Zhuhai, according to the report.
CFM International's November 6 announcement confirms China Eastern's engine selection for 101 aircraft, together with spare engines and a long-term services agreement. CFM is a 50/50 joint venture between GE Aerospace and Safran Aircraft Engines.
The aircraft will include A320neo, A321neo and A321XLR models, CFM said, without providing an individual delivery schedule in its announcement. It says China Eastern already operates 215 A320neo and A321neo aircraft powered by LEAP-1A engines, making the selection an extension of an established engine fleet.
The airline also uses the LEAP-1B on Boeing 737 MAX aircraft and the LEAP-1C on COMAC C919s, according to CFM. These are distinct engine variants for different aircraft platforms; the spare-engine agreement spans both newer LEAP models and the older CFM56-7B.
MTU's Zhuhai facility description lists LEAP and CFM56 maintenance capabilities . Its separate Jinwan branch, operating since March 2025, focuses on Pratt & Whitney PW1100G-JM engines.
GE's latest financial results show the scale of the servicing opportunity. In its third-quarter results released October 20 , the company reported a commercial-services backlog exceeding US$170bn. Commercial Engines & Services revenue from services grew 17% year over year in the quarter; spare-parts revenue rose more than 20%.
CFM is also preparing for more LEAP maintenance as the installed fleet grows. Its July maintenance-network update described five-year investment commitments exceeding US$1bn by GE Aerospace and €1bn by Safran Aircraft Engines, alongside expansion of licensed maintenance providers and spare-parts inventories.
Those investments address the support needed after engines are delivered. For airlines, access to replacement engines, parts and repair slots can matter alongside the original purchase price. Airways has examined how engine-maintenance bills can remain elevated even as aircraft availability improves .
Neither CFM's announcement nor Reuters' account supplies a breakdown showing how the US$12.9bn total is divided between engine sales, spare engines and future maintenance.

articles.title_orig: How midterm elections sent Wall Street from celebration to mayhem in just 24 hours / this week
articles.title_zh: How midterm elections sent Wall Street from celebration to mayhem in just 24 hours / this week
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street's tumultuous midterm election week kicked off with a celebration among investors.
On Wednesday, stocks soared after Democrats swept both chambers of Congress. The Dow ( ^DJI ) surged more than 1,500 points. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) rallied nearly 2%.
And in less than 24 hours, stocks reversed course , plunging Thursday as Wall Street and Main Street investors alike ditched artificial intelligence winners and chip stocks, sending the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) into correction territory.
The extraordinary reversal marked just the latest whipsaw in a year of wild swings, with the market's best expectation of future volatility, the VIX ( ^VIX ), spiking to its highest level since President Trump extended the deadline for the Iran war in late March.
As the election results rolled in, Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, was glued to his television, flipping between CNN, Fox, MSNBC, and Bloomberg while watching stock futures slip. When Sosnick went to bed, futures were still down roughly 1%.
Democrats had won control of both the House and Senate , resolving one major source of uncertainty for markets, while introducing a specific complication to the country's artificial intelligence investment boom.
States where newly elected governors have promised to stop or pause data center construction account for an estimated 45% of planned US data center capacity, according to Goldman Sachs.
In Texas, where more than half of the country's data center capacity is planned for construction, stakes were especially high. Democrat Gina Hinojosa had just won the race to become governor after promising a moratorium on new data center approvals.
The shift caught the attention of one of the world's most prominent business titans.
"Data centers in space look pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk posted on X early Wednesday.
By Wednesday morning, Wall Street was seeing silver linings in the blue wave.
Stocks took off. The Dow jumped 3%, its best day in months. The S&P 500 rose 1.6%, and the Nasdaq gained 1.4%.
Investors appeared to welcome the prospect of a divided government, potentially limiting some of President Trump's agenda. Oil prices ( CL=F , BZ=F ) also plunged, helping ease inflation concerns.
And the removal of election uncertainty ushered in a sharp drop in the VIX. That drop may have encouraged volatility-sensitive trading strategies to buy stocks, adding more upward pressure to the rally, according to Sosnick. As prices climbed, more investors piled in.
But beneath the rally, trouble was brewing.
For more than a month, hedge funds had been selling stocks tied to the artificial intelligence boom in a dash to lock in year-end profits. Shares of chipmaking equipment companies Lam Research ( LRCX ) and Applied Materials ( AMAT ) had already lost roughly a third of their value over the preceding month.
The prospect of a blue sweep bringing new data center restrictions was just one more reason to retreat from the AI trade .
By Thursday, those strains became impossible to ignore. The Dow plunged more than 1,800 points, wiping out Wednesday's gains. The S&P 500 sank 4.4%. The Nasdaq collapsed 5.5%.
Truist chief markets strategist Keith Lerner described the moves to clients as "something of a buyers' strike" in tech stocks.
The VIX volatility index ( ^VIX ) spiked as much as 70% , a move that has only happened eight times since 1991, according to data from CBOE.
" They're shooting the generals ," Nomura strategist Charlie McElligott wrote Thursday, describing the unraveling of the year's most popular stock market bets.
For Sosnick, stocks' reversal illustrated how quickly investor confidence can evaporate.
The election results hadn't changed. What had changed was investors' willingness to take risks. And in a market already questioning the AI boom, that was enough to turn Wednesday's celebration into Thursday's rout. At Friday's close, the S&P posted its worst weekly performance since June.
Follow David Hollerith on X @DsHollers .

articles.title_orig: Inside the Operation That Helped Ukraine Reverse Some Russian War Gains
articles.title_zh: Inside the Operation That Helped Ukraine Reverse Some Russian War Gains
articles.content_orig:
In the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk direction , as we noted in our previous sitrep, the situation has stabilized, and the advance of Russian assault troops around the town of Mykolaivka has effectively come to a halt. This is confirmed by new posts from the pro-Russian Slivochny Kapriz project, featuring geolocated footage of Russian strikes on Ukrainian positions in the villages of Piskunivka , Rai-Oleksandrivka , and Tykhonivka .
In the context of Operation Vivaldi, the 3rd Army Corpsâ use of ground robots equipped with grenade launchers was discussed . Now, footage has emerged showing a large-scale assault involving such robots, apparently in the Lyman direction , judging by the reference to the Russian Armed Forcesâ 3rd Motorized Rifle Division, which is part of the 20th Combined Arms Army. Pro-Russian sources report that 28 robots were destroyed by drones. On the one hand, launching such a large-scale robot assault without cover from friendly drones looks like a mistake. On the other, it may have been used as a diversion while assault infantry approached Russian positions along a different route.
The pro-Russian Slivochny Kapriz project has published its estimate of the Russian Armyâs advance in October, according to which the RuAF captured an additional 7.25 kmÂ² of territory. This is virtually zero compared with September, when the project recorded an advance of 177 kmÂ². We had expected that, if the trend observed in the first half of the month continued, the project would record a net loss of territory for the first time in several years of tracking. We do not know which territorial gains were included in the calculation to produce a positive figure.
Notably, these figures are close to the territorial gains by the AFU reported by Volodymyr Zelenskyy: 10.4 kmÂ² in October. At present, the Russian advance is approaching zero when the territorial gains of both sides are taken into account. Starting in November, the pace of offensive operations is expected to decline further with the onset of colder weather and the loss of foliage.
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) reported on its Telegram channel that UAV operators of the Alpha Special Operations Center killed 2,146 Russian soldiers and wounded another 1,052 over the course of a week. This would amount to approximately 300 Russian soldiers killed per day, or more than 9,000 per month if extrapolated. This represents a substantial increase compared Ð° with figures reported in previous months: 6,000 âneutralizedâ in July and August , and 7,600 in September . The SBU claims that this particular unit leads the Ukrainian Defense Forces in the number of enemy targets struck.
Meanwhile, the Unmanned Systems Forces reported that their drones killed approximately 300 Russian soldiers per day in October, which would amount to another roughly 9,000 killed per month. This means that just two formations reportedly account for 18,000 Russian soldiers killed per month.
In our assessment, the RuAF's total irrecoverable losses (those killed in action, permanently disabled personnel, prisoners of war, and deserters) may amount to approximately 25,000-30,000 personnel per month. If the Unmanned Systems Forces and Alpha alone account for 18,000 KIA, less than half of Russia's total irrecoverable losses would be left to account for all other categories of irrecoverable losses and the results of operations by all other Ukrainian military branches, including artillery. If our estimate were incorrect and Russian losses actually reached nearly 50,000 per month, as claimed by various sources, the situation for the RuAF along the frontline would already be critical, as losses would significantly exceed recruitment levels (approximately 30,000 personnel per month). In that scenario, we would expect to see a genuine collapse of the frontline rather than the current situation, in which Ukrainian and Russian territorial advances are roughly comparable.
One argument supporting the credibility of Ukrainian figures on Russian losses is the e-points system and the verification of strikes through the Delta situational awareness system. However, we see no reason to assume that publicly released reports necessarily correspond to the actual statistics of units recorded in the internal system.
Michael Kofman is also skeptical of some Ukrainian public claims. In a podcast with a serviceman from the AFU's 3rd Corps, Kofman asked him not to cite an unrealistic casualty ratio between the two sides.
The Economist has estimated that between 374,000 and 770,000 Russian military personnel have been killed, with total casualties, including the wounded, estimated at between 1.4 million and 2.1 million. Many Russian-language media outlets ran headlines featuring only the upper bound, even though the difference between the upper and lower estimates exceeds the lower estimate itself, making it incorrect to present 770,000 as an established death toll. For comparison, by Oct. 30, BBC News Russian and the independent Russian media outlet Mediazona, together with volunteers, had established the names of 285,023 killed Russian soldiers. If we still assume that open sources account for 45-55% of deaths and that our previous formula works (though we no longer believe this to be the case), the actual number of Russian military personnel killed would be approximately 520,000. Due to high drone activity and an extremely low rate of advance, the recovery of bodies from the gray zone is difficult, and deaths are recorded in obituaries and government registries only after substantial delays. Therefore, a more complete picture of casualties for 2026 will likely emerge only in a year or two. The estimate of "around half a million killed" appears plausible, but the available data do not allow us to confirm or rule out The Economist's upper estimate of 770,000.
The humanitarian operation in occupied Oleshky ended on the evening of Nov. 1. According to the latest figures , about 750 people were evacuated from the town (both sides decided not to disclose the exact number). Most of those who wanted to leave went to Ukraine, traveling by air from Anapa to Gomel and then by bus through Belarus. Some residents chose to go to Russian-controlled territory. Thousands of people remain in the town and its outskirts, so humanitarian missions need to continue.
The General Staff of the AFU and other Ukrainian military officials said Russian forces used the ceasefire to rotate personnel and bring up equipment and munitions. This does not, however, suggest that Russia is preparing an offensive against the city of Kherson : the Dnipro remains a formidable obstacle, and Russian troops cannot supply a large force on the river's right bank. Earlier, Sky News, citing Ukrainian marines, also reported ceasefire violations by the RuAF and published footage purportedly showing the violations. However, Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, did not confirm these allegations.
Yana Lantratova, the Russian Commissioner for Human Rights, said the Russian side is doing everything it can to help citizens and protect their rights. But Russia, as the occupying power, bears direct responsibility for protecting civilians who remain in Oleshky and for meeting their basic needs. Russian authorities could have evacuated residents from the dangerous area near the front line much earlier. The evacuation should continue even after the joint humanitarian operation has ended.
The US State Department has approved the sale of 500 PAC-3 MSE interceptor missiles to Ukraine for $2.1 billion, but deliveries are not expected before 2030. To obtain the munitions sooner, Ukrainian officials are proposing that the United States and other partners transfer PAC-3 missiles from existing allied stockpiles and replenish them later with missiles produced under the new contract. Such an exchange is technically feasible, but it requires a political decision by the US administration

articles.title_orig: IRGC claims a self-imposed limit on ballistic missile range ‘has been lifted’
articles.title_zh: IRGC claims a self-imposed limit on ballistic missile range ‘has been lifted’
articles.content_orig:
Iran is building underground military complexes able to sustain weapons production and storage even under heavy bombardment, according to the country’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) .
IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi made a series of announcements on Saturday about the military’s capabilities during a news conference in Tehran, Iranian media reported.
Among the achievements listed were an “underground missile city” set to be unveiled, the semi-official Tasnim news agency reported.
Mohebbi said the IRGC had rapidly transferred its missile and drone production lines from the surface to underground facilities. This allows Iran to continue producing missiles while its adversaries assumed its stockpiles were dwindling, he explained.
The spokesperson also outlined advances in stealth technology. He maintained that such improvements had allowed Iran’s missiles and drones to pierce air defence systems and accurately strike targets during previous rounds of fighting with the United States and Israel.
“Today, every weapon used by the IRGC Aerospace Force is manufactured using homegrown knowledge and expertise. Moreover, our products are not even derived from reverse-engineering captured enemy war material,” Iran’s IRNA news agency quoted Mohebbi as saying.
A recent report by US newspaper, The Wall Street Journal, shows that Iran caused billions of dollars in damage to US bases throughout the Middle East during previous rounds of fighting.
Meanwhile, a separate report by the Reuters news agency found that Iran had successfully targeted Gulf infrastructure on at least 135 occasions during the same period, causing billions of dollars in damage and lost revenues.
Mohebbi also warned on Saturday that restrictions on the range of Iranian missiles had been lifted. The warning follows a statement from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who said that there would be “ no geographical limits ” to Iran’s response if it were attacked again by the US and Israel.
The US-Israeli war on Iran was launched on February 28, prompting Tehran to close the Strait of Hormuz and triggering a global energy crisis. Mediation efforts have stepped up recently, as regional countries hope to bring the war to an end.
On Friday, President Donald Trump said the US military launched limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, while also claiming Washington had made “a lot of progress” in talks with Iran.
Tehran has repeatedly warned that it will target Gulf energy infrastructure if the fighting resumes. Such attacks would likely push energy prices even higher.
Meanwhile, Washington has also imposed additional sanctions on Iran as it seeks to force Tehran to concede to its demands. The restrictions have further strained the country’s economy, forcing Iran to adopt new trade routes.
On Saturday, US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced it was establishing a new task force that will support ongoing US efforts to prevent Iran from using land routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials.
The US has also imposed a naval blockade on Iran to prevent it from exporting oil.

articles.title_orig: The tech billionaires who fled California are facing a new blue Texas
articles.title_zh: The tech billionaires who fled California are facing a new blue Texas
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.
Democrats’ historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could also have a dramatic effect on the tech industry.
In dozens of local ballot measures, voters rejected data centers . And even when they weren’t voting on the issue directly, they were electing politicians — like Texas’ new governor-elect Gina Hinojosa — who campaigned on the promise of restricting data centers.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed what the midterms mean for the tech industry. Sean kicked it off by noting that Elon Musk “seems to have basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars” to Republicans, while his companies are now headquartered “in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn.”
And Kirsten said that while data centers probably weren’t the main cause of the “blue wave,” they’ve become an “an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about” getting their projects approved. And now, “we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, ‘Actually, we can change our policies.’”
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity.
Sean O’Kane: First off, let’s talk about the fact that one of the biggest data center builders was also the largest donor to the Republican Party. Elon Musk seems to have gotten basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars — maybe even more, by the time we see the final count — and in fact is now sitting there with all of his businesses in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn for the first time in a very long time, if ever.
That, I think, is the biggest thing hanging above a lot of this discussion. But, there were also a bunch of ballot measures up around the country that would have paved the way for data centers to get built faster. Almost all of them got shot down, or voted against. [Actually, many of the ballot measures would have imposed restrictions or moratoriums on data centers, and almost all of those measures passed.]
With [Democrats] in power, there is a consensus view, at least in the tech world, that this is going to mean we have a lot of roadblocks ahead for data centers, especially in places like Texas, where [you have] folks like the governor-elect [Gina] Hinojosa, who has spoken pretty openly about this being a campaign promise and something that she wants to focus on once she takes power, now that she’s beaten Greg Abbott.
It’s the thing that I think the tech world is maybe a little too focused on. I’m curious what you guys think about that.
Anthony Ha: I don’t necessarily think that they’re too focused on it, but I understand why it would feel a little bit disproportionate — the data center ballot measures, certainly there were a number of them, but it wasn’t something that was on the ballot everywhere.
And in different races, the dynamic might have been a bit different, but there was this undercurrent and sense that it seems to be an issue that reaches across the country, that is bipartisan in a lot of ways, but that the Democrats seem to have been more effective at harnessing that energy. And of course, there’s all kinds of reasons why the Democrats did so well on Tuesday, but it does seem like anti-AI and especially anti-data center sentiment was a big part of it. That seems like a pretty potent political force.
The next two years, [and] potentially beyond that, are going to be more difficult for tech companies in general, and hyperscalers, data center companies in particular. I also imagine that they have to be a little bit worried about: Is this going to continue to be an issue, not just with the people who got elected this year, but potentially in 2028 and beyond?
Kirsten Korosec: Absolutely. I don’t think that the data center issue is what brought everyone to the polls and led to the quote-unquote “blue wave.” However, I will say that data centers have been an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about getting these data centers [approved] — very secretive, oftentimes requiring NDAs of a elected officials or appointed officials, not sharing information about the scale of a project in very environmentally sensitive areas, including in the Southwest, where there’s very much a water scarcity issue.
So I think that a lot of folks — Republicans, independents, and Democrats —  all saw this as wrong. They were motivated by it, but I don’t think it was a singular issue.
Now, here’s the interesting thing. There was a lot of waving of hands about how [AI companies] can’t possibly operate under any other circumstances. And we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, “Actually, we can change our policies.” They just released what they call a compute campus policy blueprint . And guess what? They’re not going to require NDAs anymore. They’re going to share their plans and supposedly operate in less secrecy.
I think what this shows is that when you put up either a regulatory certainty in the marketplace, or at least signals of going in that direction, then corporations will respond. If you don’t do that, they will not necessarily do the thing that we hope that they will do.
Anthony: One thing I want to emphasize is that they’re calling it this [their] “compute campus policy.” And part of what that’s doing, beyond laying out these policy changes, is also an attempt to rebrand data centers, because they have become such a toxic phrase. So they’re not data centers anymore, they are compute campuses, and I’m curious, whether either of you think that’ll take.
Sean: I mean, this is ridiculous. Come on. It’s not going to change anything. It’s going to cause them more effort. For a company that likes to say that it’s no longer focused on side quests, OpenAI still loves to go in different directions a lot. And this is just the latest kind of thing where it’s just like: Why are you spending time on this at all? It doesn’t really seem like it’s going to move the needle.
Kirsten: I have a great idea for OpenAI. Because in the spirit of making threatening things seem cute, they should 100% create a compute campuses avatar, [a] cutesy thing, and then just present that instead of a power-, energy-sucking, water-sucking data center.
Anthony: And if these are just lovely compute campuses, they should just build their own offices there or work next door, see how that works out for them.
Something else that I’m wondering about is, to what extent the election is maybe the second part of a one-two punch. [We’ve just seen] a big shift in how Wall Street is reacting to a lot of these hyperscalers and AI companies and this sense that [investors] are not excited about the idea that they should be spending all this money building new data centers, spending all this money on compute. And so there’s a financial incentive not to build all these data centers.
I’m very curious how that’s going to play out. [From a regulatory standpoint,] it’s probably going to be harder to build data centers. Wall Street is probably not going to reward you for building data centers. But at the same time, to get to the scale that they want to get to, they are probably going to need to build data centers somewhere.

articles.title_orig: Binance Says Kaiser Ng Leaving, Names Justin Yek New CFO
articles.title_zh: Binance Says Kaiser Ng Leaving, Names Justin Yek New CFO
articles.content_orig:
Binance said hackers used fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to infiltrate its wallet infrastructure, leading to the record-breaking Oct. 29 cyberattack that resulted in more than $6 billion in assets being stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange.
The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop.
"In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added. "In September they posed as recruiters and ran a series of job interviews with another engineer, and that ended up in a coding exercise that contained hidden malware designed to evade security ... from there they moved violently through our internal AI tools and obtain[ed] access that breach[ed] the system that authorized our wallet transaction."
He also said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.
Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group.
Preparations for the attack began in June, when a Binance Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation "to install a popular AI coding tool after searching for it on a search engine," according to a security report published by Binance Tuesday. It said it detected the suspicious activity, replaced the engineer's device and rotated credentials as a precaution, but that by then the employee's "role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker."
As Binance works to recover from the incident, it has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets. Binance and industry partners including Tether, Circle and Ripple have reportedly frozen about $3 billion in assets, though some stolen funds continue to move through laundered channels. Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.
Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack.
The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges. Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges.
As of Tuesday Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool, replaced compromised devices, decommissioned credentials and tokens associated with the affected engineers and expanded security scans across employee devices, Teng told "Squawk on the Street."
"We're also getting an independent expert to review everything that we have done, and we'll keep strengthening our defenses as the investigation continues," Teng said. "We're working around the clock with law enforcement agencies and with industry partners to trace and freeze the stolen funds for that front."

articles.title_orig: A ‘Chaotic Race’ for the World’s Top Diplomat
articles.title_zh: A ‘Chaotic Race’ for the World’s Top Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
Meanwhile, Turkey's newly nominated Feridun Sinirlioğlu drew eight discouragement votes in his debut poll
Noushad Thekkayil/NurPhoto via Getty Images
Rebeca Grynspan, speaks during the opening ceremony of the 9th World Investment Forum (WIF 2026) in Doha, Qatar, on October 25, 2026.
Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan recorded another strong showing in the race for United Nations secretary-general on Thursday, increasing her support in the eighth Security Council straw poll, while Turkey’s newly nominated candidate struggled in his debut and the established front-runners maintained their positions.
Thursday’s straw poll again used undifferentiated ballots, concealing whether votes came from the five permanent, veto-wielding members — the U.S., United Kingdom, France, Russia and China — or the council’s 10 elected members. The selection process has also been shaped by informal regional rotation norms and calls for the U.N. to select its first female leader. The latest result shows that the newcomers took nothing from the front-runners, while Grynspan appears to be consolidating support.
Grynspan, a former Costa Rican vice president who would become the first woman and first Jewish person to lead the U.N. if selected, had her best day of the race, receiving 12 encouragement votes and three discouragement votes, according to reported results of the confidential ballot. Her showing improved from the previous round, when she received 11 encouragement votes and four discouragement votes.
However, the race is not yet settled as questions remain about whether she has overcome potential vetoes from permanent Security Council members. The last color-coded round, held Oct. 16, showed that Grynspan, International Atomic Agency head Rafael Grossi and Guyanese diplomat Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett had each drawn two discouragement votes from permanent members. Grynspan has since lowered her total discouragement count from five to three, but the latest results do not clarify whether any opposing permanent members have changed their stance.
The results also suggest that the entry of two Middle Eastern candidates has done little to disrupt the established front-runners. Feridun Sinirlioğlu, a former Turkish foreign minister and U.N. ambassador nominated by Ankara last week, received just three encouragement votes and eight discouragement votes, with four members expressing no opinion.
Sinirlioğlu’s nomination added diplomatic nuance to the race, given President Donald Trump’s relationship with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, who remains highly critical of the Jewish state, and the administration’s efforts to defend Israel at the U.N. His initial straw poll preceded his scheduled town hall with the General Assembly on Friday and an informal dialogue with the Security Council on Monday.
Meanwhile, Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE’s former ambassador to the U.N., received seven encouragement votes, six discouragement votes and two “no opinion” votes — identical to her debut in the previous round.
Nusseibeh’s stagnant tally comes amid scrutiny over the UAE’s alleged support for the Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary group accused of committing atrocities in Sudan’s civil war. The UAE has denied providing military aid to the group. Nusseibeh has condemned RSF atrocities, expressed support for U.N. accountability efforts and stressed that she would serve independently of the Emirati government if selected.
The controversy has intensified following a New York Times report detailing findings from a confidential U.N. report concerning the UAE’s alleged role in recruiting and deploying Colombian mercenaries to support the RSF in Sudan’s civil war.
In addition, an investigation by the Foundation for Defense of Democracies found an online campaign opposing Nusseibeh’s candidacy had ties to individuals with Sudanese and Turkish interests, though it did not establish that either government directed the effort. It remains unclear how heavily the controversies have weighed on Security Council assessments.

articles.content_orig:
Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reports on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's response to Russian attacks, warning that strikes on their infrastructure will meet a painful response.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Monday that Russia is preparing a "massive attack" on Ukraine centered on Tuesday's midterm elections in the United States, accusing Moscow of seeking to exploit the historical vote to unleash strikes while the world's attention is elsewhere.
The Ukrainian leader's warning came as voters prepared to decide which party controls Congress, a result that could also influence Washington's future response to Russian President Vladimir Putin's almost five-year war in Ukraine.
In a post on X, Zelenskyy went on to urge the Trump administration to increase pressure on Moscow, warning that Russia could exploit the elections to target Ukraine's battered energy infrastructure and supply routes.
DRONE STRIKE SINKS SHIP IN NATO WATERS AS ZELENSKYY WARNS OF LOOMING ‘MASSIVE STRIKE’
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. (Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool Photo/Efrem Lukatsky/AP)
"We have intel that Russia is preparing a new massive attack on our country – primarily targeting energy and logistics," Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.
"The assumption is basically that tomorrow the world will be watching the American midterms, and what is happening here in Ukraine, along with our difficulties with air defense and Patriot missiles, will be overlooked."
Zelenskyy's warning came hours after Russian forces struck a school being used to distribute humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha, a settlement in southeastern Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region.
At least 26 people, including police officers and first responders, were killed, five others were injured and others remained missing, according to the Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda .
ZELENSKYY PRESSURES US AND EUROPE FOR MORE 'AIR DEFENSE' ASSISTANCE AMID ONGOING WAR WITH RUSSIA
Ukraine's largest private energy company reports 90% of generation capacity damaged by Russian attacks, leaving over 1 million without power during freezing temperatures. (Reuters)
In his X post, Zelenskyy urged the U.S. and its allies to warn Putin that continued attacks on Ukraine would bring serious economic consequences.
"We need signals from the world to Russia that will make them feel that terror is no good, that it will bring no gains, and that as long as this war continues, their oil will burn, and they will not be able to make money doing business with the world," Zelenskyy warned.
"We must not play games with Russia's oil or gas revenues," he added.
"We must put pressure on Russia in such a way that it has no alternative but to end this war. America can do this."
TRUMP ANNOUNCES IMMEDIATE ENERGY CEASEFIRE BETWEEN RUSSIA AND UKRAINE
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left talks with President Donald Trump and members of his Cabinet during a lunch meeting at the White House on Oct. 17, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has sought to negotiate an end to the war with the help of special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner , both of whom have been involved in diplomatic efforts with Moscow.
Zelenskyy told Fox News in a Sunday interview that Ukraine would suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries for a month if Washington provided Patriot missile interceptors during the same period, potentially opening the door to diplomacy.
The State Department approved the potential sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptor missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion, according to Reuters.
The proposed sale could provide a significant boost to Ukraine's air defenses if finalized, although the delivery timeline is uncertain.
TRUMP SAYS US WILL LET UKRAINE MAKE PATRIOT MISSILES IN MAJOR POLICY SHIFT
First Lady Melania Trump, left, and civilians being evacuated from Oleshky, Ukraine, in October 2022 during the early days of the Russia-Ukraine war. (Umit Bektas/Reuters; Alexander Ermochenko/Reuters)
On Monday, Ukraine also accused Moscow of exploiting a U.S.-backed humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky , in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, to strengthen Russian military positions.
Nearly 800 people were evacuated during the six-day humanitarian pause, according to first lady Melania Trump, with the White House clarifying that she helped broker the arrangement.
Ukraine's General Staff accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian pause to rotate troops, reinforce their defenses and improve battlefield logistics.
"Under the ceasefire introduced for the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, units of the Defence Forces of Ukraine ensured that the ceasefire was observed and acted exclusively within the framework of the agreements reached," the General Staff said in a statement on X.

"The enemy, by contrast, used the humanitarian pause to improve its positions."

articles.title_orig: Mass Effect 3’s Co-op Multiplayer Is Revived with Legendary Edition Multiplayer Mod on N7 Day, Even as BioWare’s Closure Hangs Over the Celebration
articles.title_zh: Mass Effect 3’s Co-op Multiplayer Is Revived with Legendary Edition Multiplayer Mod on N7 Day, Even as BioWare’s Closure Hangs Over the Celebration
articles.content_orig:
When the Mass Effect Legendary Edition came out in 2021, it included the single player campaign of all three original games, along with all the DLC. But while all the story content you could ever want was included, Mass Effect 3's multiplayer mode was conspicuously absent, despite having a dedicated fanbase.
Now, just a few weeks after EA's shutdown of BioWare , a team of modders has successfully ported Mass Effect 3 's multiplayer to the Legendary Edition, with all the graphics and engine improvements that came with that re-release. The mod will be coming out on N7 Day – November 7th – and will be free to play, as long as you already own Mass Effect Legendary Edition.
I also got a chance to sit down with Mgamerz, who runs the ME3Tweaks team that created the mod, to talk about Mass Effect 3, and about the state of modding in 2026. And if you want to download the mod yourself, it's available now on Nexus Mods.
IGN: So, tell me a little bit about the project, and how you got started on basically porting the Mass Effect 3 multiplayer over to the Legendary Edition.
Mgamerz: Yeah, so my dev team, ME3Tweaks, and I run it. We ported Pinnacle Station back in 2021. Crazy effort. I don't know how we got that done in a two-month timeframe. And then we were doing other projects for two years, and then near the end of me working on LE2 Randomizer, which is a randomizer for legendary Mass Effect 2, someone discovered a copy of the Citadel in Mass Effect 2.
There's an area from the wards. I can't remember which game it was, but they found an area of the game that nobody knew about before, and you could load into and you're like, 'Well, this was clearly supposed to be something, and then they just never finished it.' It was a very early prototype. And it was like, 'Man, what if we could port something like that into another level?' And so I made this project called Project Wardle, Ward being the first part of it. (We have a bunch of stupid internal code names.)
And I eventually made it so we could port a Mass Effect 2 level into Mass Effect 3, and we fixed up the cover, because cover is just an unbelievable nightmare. It's very important for enemies to be able to use it. Gameplay's a huge component of why Mass Effect 3 is fun. And we got that working and then I was like, 'Well, man, what if we could port the multiplayer levels?' Because we did it for Pinnacle Station. We ported the old game. But Pinnacle Station is mostly just reused assets from Mass Effect 1.
Like 90% of it was just existing assets that they just reused. But multiplayer was totally different. It's like, yeah, none of this content exists. So the scope of work is just huge. So at the end of 2023, right as we finished LE2 Randomizer, literally on N7 day, I spun up a new Discord.
I invited a couple people and they're like, 'What's this Discord about?' I'm like, 'We're going to do something stupid. We're going to port [Mass Effect 3] Multiplayer.' And those were the first two messages I ever sent. I have some screenshots of it.
And then people were like, 'Yeah, you're joking, right?' And I'm like, 'No.' And then the last three years we've been working on it. It hasn't been constant. Last year I broke my arm, which set us back six to eight months.
But for the first two years, it was tons of prototyping. Within the first month of this project, we actually had multiplayer working. It was a proof of concept. And then we spent the next two years getting audio to port, from a different version of the audio engine because they upgraded it. It's like we got shaders building, which was a total nightmare because BioWare compiled the game with a bunch of sources that don't ship with the game.
And so we had to figure out 'how do we replicate that?' So that took a long time. And then it's like textures. We have a bunch more people that know how to do texture upscaling. The first two years is almost all prototype and then asset generation. We want to make it look good. We're planning stuff out, that kind of stuff. So that's really not how it started.
IGN: So, you basically built from scratch again? Did you take assets from the original Mass Effect 3?
Mgamerz: Oh yeah, the whole thing ports from it. It's not a one-to-one port. We're not just taking Mass Effect 3 multiplayer and dumping it into Legendary Edition and then, 'Hey guys, check out it's multiplayer, [as] you remember it.' Where we took a lot of extra steps, the lighting actually gets re-baked in Unreal Engine 4's light solver.
Essentially what that means is, imagine you have a light bulb in a room and if you wanted to project what the lights would look like, a light beam's going to hit your microphone and it's going to cast a shadow.
And then that light bounces off for you, goes into your closet and it bounces off and illuminates the closet a little bit from the inside. Unreal Engine 3 had a solver and that's how all of the lighting for all the Unreal Engine 3 games worked. But in Unreal Engine 4, they added like, 'Oh, we can do additional light bounces or we found a better statistical way to do light bounces.' And so you get crisper shadow edges or the more soft, like a grate covering on some maps. The light bounces through the grate, and unless you have super high resolution textures, it looks terrible. Mass Effect 3 is full of terrible light maps. If you look at them, you're like, 'Wow, it's just a big stair step of shadows and it looks bad.' And so we spent a lot of time upgrading that kind of stuff.
I modded Mass Effect 3 multiplayer for eight years before Legendary Edition came out, and there's a bunch of stuff I was like, 'Wow, I didn't even realize three of the character classes don't even use the highest-quality mesh.' So it's like BioWare made the Geth Infiltrator, and they made it at a high quality where it has all the polygons and triangles. And then as you get further away from the camera, it gets less triangles, because you can't see as much detail. But BioWare was just like, 'We're just not going to use the highest quality one. We'll ship it in the game, but you'll never see it.' And so it's like, 'Oh, well, we can just turn those on and it's an immediate quality upgrade.'
IGN: Was quality a big reason why you took on this massive undertaking to bring ME3 multiplayer to Legendary Edition? Because if I understand correctly, the servers for the original ME3 multiplayer are still working, for now at least.
Mgamerz: By the time we publish this, I don't know, man. N7HQ's gone, so I wouldn't be surprised if it disappears before.
Actually, the whole reason this project started, I was getting to the end of LE2 Randomizer and I was like, 'Man, I love Mass Effect 3 multiplayer.' I modded tons of stuff into it, and it was really fun.
I went back and I was like, 'I want to make a new one. I want to make a new mod.' I went back to it and I was like, 'These tools,' and I'm totally throwing myself under the bus, 'These tools suck. There's no debug tools. Everything is so immature compared to what we have in Legendary Edition, thanks to what BioWare changed for us.' And so I was like, 'Man, I'd rather just port multiplayer than have to deal with this awful development environment.'
And then I was like, 'Okay, well, I've modeled this forever.' I know where all of the pain points are in extending this because I made a new map pack, I made a new enemy pack that adds a new faction. So I'm like, 'I know where all the landmines were, because I had to pioneer it.' And I'm like, 'What if we rebuilt multiplayer and accounted for those landmines so if someone else wants to do it, they don't have to go through the same landmines, or they're at least aware that they're there?' So there's a bunch of considerations for extensibility.
As a user, if you just go in and you just play Standard, you might not notice the changes, but the next dev who wants to add a new faction, it'll be like, 'Wow, I don't have to deal with all these stupid problems that I would've had in the o

articles.title_orig: Microsoft Researcher John Langford Exits as AI Frontiers Group Is Declared Finished
articles.title_zh: Microsoft Researcher John Langford Exits as AI Frontiers Group Is Declared Finished
articles.content_orig:
John Langford, a partner researcher manager at Microsoft Research New York, has left Microsoft.
He declared the AI Frontiers group over, according to Digg , which summarised a post on his blog, Machine Learning (Theory). Langford announced the post on social media on Nov. 6.
The group had about 50 people. It was moved out of Microsoft Research and into Microsoft AI in early September.
Langford wrote that he found places for his team members as well as he could before leaving, Digg reported.
His account does not detail the group's formal status or where remaining staff were assigned.
Langford wrote that he and colleagues created AI Frontiers inside Microsoft Research in 2023. They wanted more organized research after the release of ChatGPT.
Much of the group's work centred on making AI agents function reliably.
Projects he named include Autogen, a framework for coordinating agents. Another is Fara, an agent that operates a computer to carry out tasks.
Shunyatax also described some researchers in the group as exploring ways to improve models without simply making them larger.
Langford described the leadership philosophy in Microsoft AI as focused on scaling rather than research, Digg reported. He said the environment focused mainly on getting, making and refining data.
He conceded the business logic. In his assessment, returns to scale are more predictable than returns to research. Still, he called a scaling-only approach misdirected and unenjoyable, Digg reported.
Those are his judgments. They concern the unit his group joined, not company-wide policy.
Shunyatax reported that Langford's position was not that scaling should stop. It said he argued scaling and fundamental research should run side by side.
Langford wrote that he could not get innovations used, or even seriously considered, while in Microsoft AI. A return to Microsoft Research held little appeal.
He doubted research could reach use from there either.
Langford wrote, in a post Digg summarised, that he is not comfortable being at a company where his research has no path to real use.
He added that there will be no internships with the group in the coming year. He wished well to the colleagues he is leaving behind, according to Digg.
His profile on the research platform alphaxiv lists him as a founding member of Microsoft Research New York. It also names him a co-creator of the Vowpal Wabbit machine-learning library.
A 2023 Test of Time Award at The Web Conference recognised his contextual-bandit paper on personalised news recommendation. The paper describes algorithms that learn which article to show a reader.
Shunyatax placed the AI Frontiers news alongside other senior changes at Microsoft.
It cited the planned departure of former LinkedIn chief executive Ryan Roslansky from his later responsibilities over the Office and Teams divisions.
It also cited the move of former AI platform head Eric Boyd to Anthropic.
The link is unproven. Shunyatax said the material does not establish that those changes stemmed from disagreements over research strategy, or that they are linked to Langford's exit.

articles.title_orig: Are hackers targeting America’s food supply?
articles.title_zh: Are hackers targeting America’s food supply?
articles.content_orig:
Acts of greyzone aggression aim to spread panic. Europe has to show the saboteurs that we are resilient
I t was as though a ghostly hand had switched the settings on supermarket freezers across Europe from “freeze” to “defrost”. From Finland to Ireland, they suddenly began heating up , many reaching 50C and food worth millions of euros had to be thrown away. But no actual hand was needed to cause the meltdown. This was a cyber-attack, or rather a chain of attacks. Like pretty much everything else in 2026, supermarket freezers are digitally enabled. That makes them smarter and more efficient, but like everything else that is connected to the internet, it also makes them more vulnerable.
Russian hacktivists claimed they were behind some of the supermarket sabotage, but no one knows for sure. It could also be Iran, Iranian proxies, North Korea – or unaffiliated bedroom hackers. When Transport for London suffered a devastating hack two years ago, the culprits turned out to be two British teenagers . Governments regularly warn retailers and other companies about cyber-attacks and even provide cyber-defence training to businesses . The lessons of costly ransomware and cyber-attacks also mean many big organisations and retailers have become much better at keeping their payments and logistics systems safe.
But freezers present a new vulnerability. In Sweden, for example, some of the stores that were attacked this week hadn’t connected their freezers to national retailers’ systems, which have centralised protection. Now they’ve learned their lesson the hard way.
Hybrid warfare – or, to use the defence term, greyzone aggression – refers to an array of hostile acts by a country’s adversaries that fall short of full-on military conflict. Cyber-hackers also this week attempted to meddle with fridges at French blood banks, while hoax bomb threats forced commercial airliners across Europe to divert, make emergency landings or require fighter jet escort to safety.
This comes after at least two years of sporadic Kremlin-suspected arson attacks on factories, explosives-laden drones flown into airports and drone incursions into countries’ airspace. There is constant GPS interference in the skies around the Baltic Sea, highly suspicious damage to subsea cables and pipelines, disinformation spread by bot farms and repeated acts of cyber-aggression.
Saboteurs and hackers usually have two aims: the first is to disrupt, but they also want to psychologically destabilise the target societies by spreading fear. It is fortunate then that the aviation hoaxes and freezer incidents coincide with a renewed conversation across Europe about resilience. It is as if the hackers wanted to showcase the need for preparedness projects such as the UK government’s new Be Ready campaign , which launched last month.
The British campaign, which instructs people on such things as stockpiling for emergencies whether caused by climate change or state-sponsored terrorism, had been in the works for months. Ministers hesitated however, fearing that citizens would respond with cynicism or ridicule, or just wouldn’t follow the advice.
Such campaigns are commonplace elsewhere. Earthquake zones such as Tokyo and San Francisco have had them for decades. “Make a Plan. Gather Supplies. Get Connected. Get Trained,” are the San Francisco city government’s pillars of instruction .
The newest version of Sweden’s official booklet In Case of Crisis or War , distributed to every home since 2018, is even more comprehensive, with clear language about everything from civil defence duties, how to volunteer (give blood or team up with neighbours for mutual support), to what items always to have at home, and how to find out if a crisis is real or a fake warning by bots.
For several years, I have been calling on the UK to follow Sweden’s lead and send a similar instruction leaflet to UK households, only to be told by officials that doing so would cause too much panic and frighten people. A House of Lords committee heard from the chair of the UK National Preparedness Commission in March that “the bulk of the UK population is blissfully unaware” of some of the risks they face.
It turns out that British people are less cynical than their leaders had assumed. Perhaps a few minds were also changed by Covid-19, which dramatically illustrated how vulnerable globalised and open societies are to all manner of threats.
after newsletter promotion
Either way, within a week of the Be Ready campaign launching, the retailer Robert Dyas reported that weekly sales of radios had shot up by 160%. Maplin reported that sales of radios had nearly doubled and sales of power banks had more than doubled, while torch sales had soared to nearly four times the usual figure.
The puddles of defrosted ice in the supermarket aisles and stress for air travellers this week show that we need to be prepared for a very wide range of threats including power and water outages. We have already seen what happens to our complex food supply chains when global shipping lanes are suddenly disrupted. Iran’s obstruction of the strait of Hormuz following US airstrikes has given us painful food inflation and costly global oil and fertiliser shortages.
But what if the ships importing the food we eat can no longer make it to our ports? No industrialised nation grows all the food it consumes. What if the internet goes down? It’s not impossible. Even companies with the best cyber defence could fall victim to sabotage of the subsea data cables that transmit nearly all our connectivity.
This week has been a nasty preview of what could happen in future with alarming regularity. Severe disruption will come our way so simply hoping for the best is not an option. The good news is that by accepting that we need to prepare, and demonstrating that we remain strong in times of crisis, we can signal to Vladimir Putin and other rogue actors that disrupting our services is unwelcome, but ultimately it is futile.
Elisabeth Braw is a Swedish security expert and the author of The Undersea War : The International Battle for Supremacy at the Bottom of the World

articles.title_orig: Berkshire Hathaway buys back $9.6 billion of its own stock but its profits declined
articles.title_zh: Berkshire Hathaway buys back $9.6 billion of its own stock but its profits declined
articles.content_orig:
Berkshire Hathaway said Saturday it accelerated its share repurchases during the third quarter, as operating and overall profits took a hit.
The Greg Abel-led conglomerate bought back $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock. That's more than double the $4.5 billion repurchased in the second quarter and brings the company's total buybacks for 2026 to about $14.4 billion.
The sharp increase came as Berkshire's operating earnings — those from wholly-owned businesses — fell year over year, as profits from its insurance business pulled back.
Berkshire operating profits totaled $12.705 billion, down 5.8% from $13.485 billion in the year-earlier period. Insurance underwriting tumbled 43% year on year to $1.352 billion, while insurance investment income declined 14% to $2.734 billion. Berkshire's railroad, energy and manufacturing businesses all saw earnings grow year over year.
The company's overall earnings, which include Berkshire's sprawling stock market portfolio, also dropped 28% in the third quarter to $22.112 billion from $30.796 billion a year prior. Investment gains for the company fell nearly 50% to $9.407 billion.
Despite the earnings pullback, Berkshire stock has outperformed recently amid a massive rotation out of technology stocks. Class A shares are up more than 12% over the past month, while the S&P 500 has dropped 5.5% in that time. Year to date, Berkshire has gained 13%, while the broad market index is up just 7.8%.
Berkshire's five largest equity holdings remained the same in the third quarter: Alphabet , American Express , Apple , Bank of America and Coca-Cola .
Berkshire's cash hoard also grew 3% in the third quarter $377.435 billion from $365.514 billion in the second quarter. However, excluding rail and utility cash along with T-bill payables, the conglomerate's cash holdings totaled $352.3 billion, down 1.9% quarter over quarter.
— CNBC's Alex Crippen contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Airstrikes kill more than 2 dozen people near Yemen’s capital, Houthis say
articles.title_zh: Airstrikes kill more than 2 dozen people near Yemen’s capital, Houthis say
articles.content_orig:
Children were among the injured people seen being carried into a nearby hospital
Media linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen say that at least 25 people, including women and children, have been killed in airstrikes by Saudi Arabia.
There has been no comment from the Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government in Yemen.
Live video footage on Al Masirah - a television station run by the Houthis - has shown rescuers pulling bodies out of the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.
The bodies of young children can be seen among those dug out from the ruins.
The television station has also shown a number of injured people being carried on stretchers to hospital.
Saba news agency, which is also run by the Houthis, said the attack was carried out by Saudi Arabia.
The Saudis have led a coalition that has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.
The war in Yemen had been dormant for several years but reignited as a result of the Iran war.
A truce began to fall apart when Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Sanaa - which is controlled by the Houthis - to prevent an Iranian plan landing there.
The Tehran-backed Houthis subsequently targeted Abha airport in Saudi Arabia, then began hitting Saudi ships that have been using the Red Sea off the coast of Yemen as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz.
Major fighting has since resumed in Yemen between the Houthis and forces fighting for the Saudi-backed government of Yemen.
On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province, which has been the focus of much of the recent fighting, is reported to have killed 30 people.
The Houthis accused the Saudis of carrying out the strike, while government forces accused the Houthis of having fired a missile at the site.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.
The Saudis have regularly bombed Houthi positions, while the group has fired multiple missiles at targets inside Saudi Arabia, including airports and oil facilities.
Hours before the strike that hit al-Shariyah, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a missile heading towards Riyadh.
A Houthi leader, Mahdi al-Mashat, has vowed that the group will take revenge for the latest attacks in Yemen.

articles.title_orig: A Look Inside Jury Selection in U.S.S. Cole Bombing Case
articles.title_zh: A Look Inside Jury Selection in U.S.S. Cole Bombing Case
articles.content_orig:
Justice takes a painfully long time, but twenty-four years is an absolute eternity. When jury selection finally kicked off at the U.S. naval base in Cuba for the capital trial of Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, it marked a strange and heavy milestone. This is the very first death-penalty case handled by a military commission at GuantÃ¡namo Bay. If you think this process resembles a standard federal courtroom drama, you're missing the entire plot.
Al-Nashiri, accused of orchestrating the October 2000 bombing of the USS Cole that killed 17 American sailors, has been in U.S. custody since 2002. For over two decades, the case has bogged down in motions, appellate ping-pong, and profound legal battles over constitutional rights and torture. Now, military panels and defense attorneys find themselves operating in a legal twilight zone that tests the absolute limits of accountability.
You cannot understand this trial without looking at what happened before al-Nashiri ever set foot in a formal courtroom. Years ago, the defendant was subjected to CIA interrogation tactics that included waterboarding and mock executions. Those severe abuses created a massive hurdle for prosecutors.
Back in 2023, the military judge threw out confessions al-Nashiri made to investigators because those statements were fundamentally tainted by prior torture. That single ruling stripped the government of its primary direct evidence. Prosecutors have to build a capital case without the confessions that investigators spent years gathering. That forces a heavy reliance on circumstantial evidence, foreign intelligence sharing, and testimony from aging witnesses who remember an attack that happened a quarter-century ago.
Just days before prospective military jurors boarded flights to Cuba, the entire proceeding nearly ground to a halt over sanity questions. Defense forensic psychiatrists argued that decades of abuse left al-Nashiri with a traumatic brain injury and severe neurocognitive disorders, rendering him mentally incompetent to stand trial.
Army Colonel Matthew Fitzgerald, the presiding judge, ordered a sanity board evaluation. The resulting decision ruled that the defense failed to overcome the legal presumption of competence, clearing the path for the 36-member military pool to begin the painstaking process of vetting jurors. Even so, mental health appeals will likely form the bedrock of any future post-conviction challenges.
Normal federal courts handle terrorism trials with established constitutional protections, open public access, and clear precedents. GuantÃ¡namo military commissions operate under a separate, hybrid framework created specifically for war crimes and alien unprivileged enemy combatants.
Legal experts have criticized this parallel system from day one. Critics argue that ad-hoc military tribunals create an appearance of a rigged outcome, whereas supporters insist they provide necessary security and flexibility for prosecuting acts of war outside standard domestic jurisdictions. When a trial takes nearly a quarter of a century to reach a jury, public confidence takes a massive hit regardless of the verdict.
Selecting a jury for a capital case is notoriously grueling under any circumstances. Doing it with active-duty military members serving as jurors on a remote island base introduces logistics you won't find anywhere else. The proceedings will happen in structured windows, keeping press and observers restricted by tight military flight schedules.
The legal teams will spend weeks questioning service members about command influence, bias, and their knowledge of the case. Every single ruling handed down right now establishes precedents that will haunt military law for generations. This isn't just about one man or one tragic bombing. It's a live stress test of whether a military commission can ever deliver credible justice after decades of institutional delays and torture controversies.
Elena Coleman is a prolific writer and researcher with expertise in digital media, emerging technologies, and social trends shaping the modern world.

articles.title_orig: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
articles.title_zh: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
articles.content_orig:
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, on 5.
The electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Kipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests.
The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens – who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops – saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

articles.title_orig: New Zealand in political limbo after knife-edge election
articles.title_zh: New Zealand in political limbo after knife-edge election
articles.content_orig:
New Zealand election 'too close to call' - so who's won?
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests, on 5.
New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon addressed supporters in Auckland as votes were being counted
The electoral commission was not due to announce the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Hipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests.
New Zealand election 2026: What you need to know
The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens â who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops â saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins speaking to supporters
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices â for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

The Mega Millions jackpot continues to grow as there was no winner of the $505 million grand prize for the drawing held on Friday, Nov. 6. That means the drawing of Tuesday, Nov. 10 will be worth $529 million, with a cash option of $224.2 million.
The winning numbers are: 27-34-44-53-64
Along with no jackpot winner, no one matched all five white balls drawn to win a $1 million prize.
Six players matched four white balls and the Mega Ball to each win a $10,000 base prize. With the automatic multiplier attached, three players won $20,000 each and three players won $30,000 each.
A total of 300,534 winning tickets were sold in the drawing.
Mega Millions drawings are held every Tuesday and Friday at 11 p.m. ET. Five balls are drawn from a set of balls numbered 1 through 70; the Mega Ball is drawn from a set of balls numbered 1 through 24. The odds of winning the jackpot are 1 in 290 million.
